newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian government completes 1997 budget measures.
newsitem.headline: Italian government completes 1997 budget measures.

text.p: The Italian government has put the finishing touches to an end-of-year package of measures which forms the last part of the 1997 austerity budget, cabinet secretary Enrico Micheli said at the weekend.

The package is meant to raise around 4.3 trillion lire ($2.8 billion) next year out of the total budget worth 62.5 trillion lire. It is due to be rubber-stamped at a cabinet meeting on Monday and will not have to be ratified by parliament.
Parliament approved the 1997 budget last weekend, giving Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government a free hand to work out how the final 4.3 trillion lire would be brought in.

Newspapers reported on Sunday that at the heart of the package were plans to force companies to speed up payments of certain excise duties -- especially in the petrol production and distribution sectors.
This measure is expected to raise 2.0 trillion lire in 1997.
Anxious not to set off inflation, Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government is expected to keep tax rises to a minimum. However, duties on unleaded petrol and cigarettes are expected to go up.

Value-added tax on certain types of medicines is also tipped to climb to 10 percent from the current four percent. The newspaper Il Sole 24 Ore said the increase could bring one trillion lire to Treasury coffers in 1997.

The government is fighting to reduce the ratio between the public sector deficit and gross domestic product (GDP) to the three percent level demanded by the Maastricht treaty for countries wishing to join the European Union's planned single currency.
The closely watched ratio is expected to be just over seven percent this year.
Many economists believe the government will have to prepare a mini-budget in early 1997 if the magic three percent threshold is to be hit next year.
